segments.say: Nadia is sitting at a long wooden table in a small restaurant on a rainy autumn evening. Around her are four friends she has known since university, more than twenty years now. The plates have been cleared, the candles are low, and someone has just ordered one more pot of tea. Nobody wants the evening to end yet.

A quick word about Nadia before we go any further. She's imagined. She's someone we've pictured together, to keep us company tonight. She's forty-four, she teaches music at a primary school, and she has the kind of laugh that people across a room turn their heads to find. Nothing about her stands for a real person, and nothing in her evening is a case study.

And then it happens. Her friend Tom tries to pour the tea, and the lid of the pot slides off and lands in the sugar bowl with a soft little plop. That's all. It isn't clever, and it isn't really a joke. But Nadia snorts, and then Tom snorts, and within a few seconds all five of them are laughing so hard that nobody can speak.

It's the kind of laughter you can't stop even when you try. Every time it starts to fade, somebody catches somebody else's eye and it starts all over again. Nadia's cheeks ache. Her eyes are wet. A couple at the next table glance over, smile, and then, to their own surprise, begin to laugh a little too, without having seen anything at all.

We'll stay with Nadia through the rest of her evening, and the walk home afterwards, and as we go we'll follow one question all the way down. Why do we laugh? It's one of the most familiar sounds a human being makes, and one of the least understood. By the end, I hope it will feel both stranger and a little more wonderful.

show.title: Tonight, we'll explore
items: Why we rarely laugh at jokes
What laughter does to the body
A slow walk home to sleep

segments.say: Let me say how we'll do this. Every study we mention tonight is real, published research, and when I give a number, it comes from that research. Where scientists disagree, where a sample was small, or where an idea is still only a guess, I'll say so. Laughter has been studied for far less time than you might think, and many of the answers are still being worked out.

Laughter is so ordinary that we hardly ever stop to notice it. You probably laughed today, perhaps several times, and I'd guess you can't remember most of them. A small laugh at a message. A polite laugh at someone's comment. A laugh of relief when something went right. It slips in and out of our days almost without our noticing.

Think about how long you've been doing it. You laughed before you could walk. You laughed before you had a single word. Laughter came before language, both in your own life and, as we'll see, in the long history of our species. It's one of the very first ways a human being finds to say something to another human being.

show.cap: You've done this all your life

segments.say: Most of us could make a list like this. With friends and family. At small accidents, like a teapot lid in a sugar bowl. In ordinary conversation, at things that aren't really funny at all. When we're nervous, or relieved. And now and then alone, at a memory that suddenly comes back and catches us in a shop or on a train.

A long wooden table after dinner, with candles burning low, a teapot, a few cups and folded napkins, and rain on the window behind. It's the place where our evening begins. A table where nothing special was happening, until a small accident turned five grown adults into helpless, giggling children for a few minutes. Keep this table in mind as we go.

It helps to separate two questions that often get tangled together. The first is what laughter actually is, as a thing the body does: the breath, the voice, the face. The second is why we do it at all, what it's for, and why it seems to happen so much more with other people. The first question has some fairly clear answers. The second is where the real mystery lives.

show.title: Two questions, not one
items: What is laughter, in the body
Why do we do it at all

segments.say: Back at the table, Nadia is trying to get her breath back. She presses a napkin to her eyes and holds up one hand, as if to say please, no more. Tom says, quite seriously, the tea will be fine, and that sets everyone off again. The waiter arrives with the bill, sees the five of them, and wisely decides to come back later.

If she'd been asked to describe it, Nadia might have listed a few sensations. Short, sharp bursts of breath, coming whether she wanted them or not. Aching cheeks. Wet eyes. A strange weakness in her arms, as if she couldn't have lifted the teapot herself. And the odd feeling of trying to speak, and finding that the words simply would not come out.

show.title: What Nadia noticed in her body

segments.say: That's the puzzle we'll carry with us. A laugh can burst out before we've decided anything, and sometimes for no reason we could explain. It can come from joy, from nerves, from relief, or from a teapot lid. Understanding even part of how that works tells us something about how closely our bodies, our feelings and other people are tied together.

show.text: We laugh for reasons we can't always name

segments.say: Before we start, one gentle note. Nothing tonight is a rule about how anyone should laugh. Some people laugh easily and often, others more quietly, and both are normal ways of being human. This video is for learning and is not medical advice. If you notice a big change in how you laugh or feel, that's a good reason to talk to a doctor.

segments.say: So settle in, wherever you are tonight. If you'd like to listen closely, every detail is there for you. If you'd rather let the evening carry you along and drift off somewhere between the restaurant and home, that's completely fine too. There's nothing you need to remember and no test at the end. You can leave whenever sleep finds you.

show.sub: There's no test at the end

segments.say: Our first stop is a question so simple that most of us have never asked it. What is a laugh, actually? Not what makes us laugh, but the thing itself: the sound, the breath, the movement of the face. It sounds like an easy question. Let's see what the people who have listened to thousands of laughs have to say.
